curriculum.title: Social Media, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence

core.big_idea: Digital systems shape attention, speech, desire, power, and neighbour-love and therefore require moral discernment.

passages.reading_note: Observe intentional attention and rejection of corrupting influence.
Observe the relationship between what believers dwell on and what they practise.
Observe speech power, harm, inconsistency, and accountability.
Ground human dignity and tool stewardship in image-bearing.

core.metanarrative_position: Christian wisdom and witness within created culture and human tool-making.
core.biblical_genre: Psalm, epistle exhortation, and wisdom-like teaching

claims.statement: The passages call believers to intentional attention, truthful and excellent thought, disciplined practice, and accountable speech.
Applying these texts to algorithms, social media, and artificial intelligence is a prudential application rather than a direct biblical reference to modern technology.
Digital systems can influence what people attend to, say, desire, believe, and reward; therefore Christians should evaluate both personal use and system design.
claims.interpretive_hinge: The move from biblical teaching about human attention and speech to claims about how modern digital systems influence those domains.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not claim that every algorithm controls users, that all platforms have identical effects, or that a specific technical mechanism has been established without external evidence.

claims.statement: Artificial intelligence should be treated as a human-made tool and social system, not casually described as a moral person, divine oracle, or neutral source of truth.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not make unsupported claims about machine consciousness or treat an AI output as spiritual authority.

claims.statement: Responsible use should consider truth, neighbour-love, privacy, authorship, justice, human dignity, and accountability.

core.interpretation_skill: Distinguish direct biblical principle, canonical synthesis, prudential application, and unsettled technical claim.

learning.foundation_objective: Apply three biblical principles to a realistic social-media or AI scenario.
learning.extension_objective: Distinguish direct command from prudential judgment and defend a technology-use decision with explicit assumptions.
know: What each primary passage addresses in its own context.
Key ethical categories for digital systems.
understand: Technology is not morally evaluated only by whether it is new or useful.
A tool can amplify both human creativity and human sin.
practise: Run a digital case through the truth-love-stewardship-accountability grid.
Disclose AI assistance honestly where authorship matters.
become: A person whose digital habits and design choices are governed by worship of God and love of neighbour rather than appetite or convenience.
success_evidence: The student labels a statement as direct text or prudential application.
The student identifies at least two stakeholders affected by a technology decision.
The student proposes a concrete accountable practice.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students use a biblical ethics grid to evaluate social-media and AI scenarios.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: When a tool saves time, what other questions should we ask before using it?
say: The Bible does not mention recommendation algorithms or generative AI directly.
It does address attention, truth, speech, desire, neighbour-love, power, and accountability.
We must distinguish direct biblical teaching from our prudential application to a new technology.
Useful questions are: Is it true? Is it loving? Is it honest about authorship? Who gains power or bears risk? Who is accountable?
ask: What does each passage directly address?
Where are we making an application rather than quoting a command?
Who can be helped or harmed by this use?
What accountable practice would improve the scenario?
zero_prep_card.do: Work through four short cases using the Truth-Love-Stewardship-Accountability grid.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for wisdom, truthfulness, self-control, and care for neighbours in digital life.

preparation.passage_context: Psalm 101 expresses a ruler commitment to integrity; Philippians 4 gives a community pattern of thought and practice; James 3 warns teachers and believers about the disproportionate power of speech.
text_observations: The texts address human moral agency, not the mechanics of modern platforms.
Attention and speech are both formative: what people dwell on and communicate shapes life together.
James emphasizes inconsistency when praise and harm come from the same source.
interpretation_notes: Make the inference chain visible: ancient text, enduring principle, modern circumstance, prudential judgment.
Use cases that include benefits as well as risks so the lesson does not collapse into anti-technology rhetoric.
Keep technical claims modest unless separately researched and sourced.
theological_guardrails: Do not call AI inherently evil, spiritually conscious, or morally neutral without qualification.
Do not outsource pastoral, doctrinal, or safeguarding judgment to a chatbot.
Do not equate using AI assistance with dishonesty in every context; disclosure and assignment rules matter.
Do not require students to disclose private browsing history, sexual content, illegal behaviour, or mental-health conversations publicly.

likely_questions.question: Is using AI cheating?
likely_questions.purpose: Avoid an absolute answer detached from context.
likely_questions.foundation_prompt: It depends on the task, rules, disclosure, and whether the work still represents your learning.
likely_questions.extension_prompt: Distinguish assistance, substitution, plagiarism, and authorised collaboration.

likely_questions.question: Can AI be a Christian?
likely_questions.foundation_prompt: An AI system generates outputs from human-designed processes; the curriculum does not treat it as a spiritual person.
likely_questions.extension_prompt: Questions about machine consciousness are philosophically disputed and not settled by confident slogans.

likely_questions.question: Should Christians leave social media?
likely_questions.foundation_prompt: Some may leave; others may use it with limits and purpose.
likely_questions.extension_prompt: Evaluate calling, vulnerability, community, responsibilities, and fruit rather than issuing one rule for all.

essential.label: Essential
essential.use_case: Minimum viable lesson for a teacher with little preparation time or a shortened class.

outline.label: Frame
outline.instructions: Name one way a digital system can shape attention, speech, desire, or power without requesting private disclosure.

outline.label: Read
outline.instructions: Read Psalm 101:1-4, Philippians 4:8-9, and James 3:1-12 selectively.

outline.label: Build the grid
outline.instructions: Define truth, love of neighbour, stewardship, and accountability.

outline.label: Case lab
outline.instructions: Evaluate one neutral scenario with the four-part grid.

outline.label: Commit
outline.instructions: Choose one voluntary, non-disclosed practice for more truthful and responsible technology use.

standard.label: Standard
standard.use_case: Default Sunday session with reading, discussion, activity, and response.

outline.label: Frame
outline.instructions: Distinguish a tool's capability from the incentives and habits surrounding its use.

outline.label: Read
outline.instructions: Read the selected passages and derive principles without pretending they directly name modern platforms or AI.

outline.label: Build the grid
outline.instructions: Apply truth, neighbour-love, stewardship, and accountability to digital choices.

outline.label: Case lab
outline.instructions: Analyse several cases involving recommendations, synthetic media, private data, and AI-assisted work.

outline.label: Commit
outline.instructions: Draft one prudential practice and explain which biblical principles support it.

extended.label: Extended
extended.use_case: Longer session with additional textual work, activity, comparison, or assessment.

outline.label: Frame the system
outline.instructions: Map users, platforms, advertisers, creators, models, data, and incentives in a digital system.

outline.label: Read and derive
outline.instructions: Read the passages, name explicit teachings, and derive principles with evidence labels.

outline.label: Ethical grid
outline.instructions: Define truth, love, stewardship, and accountability, including disclosure when AI materially contributes.

outline.label: Case lab
outline.instructions: Use both printable resources to evaluate multiple scenarios, competing goods, and unintended consequences.

outline.label: Policy versus wisdom
outline.instructions: Separate direct moral boundaries from household, school, workplace, or congregational prudential rules.

outline.label: Commit
outline.instructions: Write one personal or group practice, its rationale, and how it can be reviewed without surveillance or forced disclosure.

discussion_questions.question: Which part of our conclusion comes directly from the passage?
How can a recommendation system shape attention without forcing a person to obey it?
When does AI assistance become dishonest authorship?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Identify assignment rules, disclosure, learning purpose, and degree of substitution.

discussion_questions.question: What responsibilities belong to users, parents, churches, schools, designers, and companies?
Which technology questions remain genuinely uncertain?

activities.title: Digital Ethics Case Lab
steps: Label conclusions as direct principle or prudential judgment.
Propose one accountable action and one unanswered question.
activities.learning_link: Moves from biblical principle to transparent moral reasoning without pretending Scripture names the technology.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Teacher reads cases aloud and students create a four-column grid on paper.

closing.prayer_prompt: Ask for truthful speech, disciplined attention, and love of neighbour in digital life.
closing.take_home_line: Use technology as an accountable neighbour, not merely as a consumer.

family.title: A Household Digital Wisdom Check
family.parent_intro: The goal is a shared ethical conversation, not surveillance or forced disclosure of private details.

flow.instructions: Name one way technology helps your household and one way it creates friction.
Choose two principles that apply to digital attention or speech.
Evaluate one neutral case, such as using AI to help draft homework or a church announcement.
Agree on one household practice and pray.

questions: What use would require disclosure to remain honest?
Who might be affected even if the tool feels private?

interactive.title: Truth-Love-Stewardship-Accountability
interactive.instructions: Choose one ordinary digital habit and score it against the four questions without demanding private disclosure.

family.weekly_action: Adopt one practice: disclose AI assistance, turn off one manipulative notification, verify before sharing, or create one device-free family period.
family.prayer: God, give us wisdom to use tools truthfully, responsibly, and for the good of our neighbours.
family.parent_note: Do not use this exercise to search devices or force disclosure. Handle serious concerns through appropriate private and safeguarding processes.

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: The Bible directly names artificial intelligence
Biblical principles can be applied prudentially to AI

answer.text: Biblical principles can be applied prudentially to AI

quiz.explanation: The inference chain should be explicit.

quiz.question: Which question primarily tests honesty of authorship?
quiz.explanation: Disclosure helps determine whether work is represented truthfully.

quiz.question: True or false: A useful tool is automatically a wise tool in every context.
quiz.explanation: Usefulness is only one ethical consideration.

quiz.question: A feed repeatedly rewards outrage. Which grid questions apply?
quiz.explanation: Truth, neighbour-love, attention stewardship, and responsibility are interconnected.

puzzle.title: Four-Question Digital Audit
puzzle.instructions: For each case, identify the strongest truth, love, stewardship, and accountability issue.
items: AI writes an assignment without disclosure
A false story is shared because it is exciting
An algorithm keeps serving angry content
A church leader uses a chatbot for a crisis response

pairs.prompt: AI writes an assignment without disclosure
A false story is shared because it is exciting
An algorithm keeps serving angry content
A church leader uses a chatbot for a crisis response

accessibility.reading_level: Teen-facing language with technical terms defined in ordinary words.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Define algorithm as a set of rules that selects or ranks outputs; define AI without implying personhood.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow written analysis instead of rapid debate.
Avoid assuming all students use the same platforms.
sensory_notes: No device use is required during the lesson.
non_reader_support: Use icons for truth, love, stewardship, and accountability.

do_not_ask: Do not ask students to reveal private messages, browsing history, sexual content, illegal activity, or chatbot conversations publicly.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Keep scenarios hypothetical. If a student discloses harm, coercion, exploitation, or immediate danger, follow local safeguarding policy rather than attempting technical or pastoral investigation in class.
safeguarding.escalation_note: D031 protocol is deferred to owner-managed work; mandatory local safeguarding duties still apply.
